transcript:
[00:00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is Samir from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:00:08] Ravi: Hey Samir, Ravi here. Aisha, Lucy, Tom with me.
[00:00:12] Elena: Elena here, Redwood SE, and Jonas from product.
[00:00:20] Samir: Great. Goal for today: deep dive into throughput tuning — continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, and we'll touch on quantization and VPC/on-prem implications.
[00:00:35] Ravi: Sounds good. Our primary measure is tokens/sec at 95th percentile latency under 350ms for single-turn generation. We're running a long prompt plus ~200 token generation, multimodal not yet.
[00:00:48] Aisha: Quick infra context: we're on k8s with AWS G5-like instances in a VPC, using private subnets. Storage is EBS, we also have an on-prem lab with A100s we might use for a PoC.
[00:01:05] Elena: cool, helps. So continuous batching as we call it is our default for high throughput — it keeps GPU warm and forms batches across requests. Two key knobs: batch_timeout (how long scheduler waits) and max_num_seqs (max concurrent sequences per batch).
[00:01:28] Tom: can you explain max_num_seqs again? we looked at docs but it's still fuzzy.
[00:01:33] Elena: Sure — it's basically the max number of sequences the runtime will pack into a single attention compute step. If you set it higher you can increase utilization but you also get longer tail latency because big batches take longer. For example max_num_seqs=8 vs 16 vs 32 — you may see 2-3x throughput improvement but 95p latency grows.
[00:01:58] Samir: also watch out for token limits: max_tokens_per_batch or global token cap. If you let long sequences pack in, they can dominate memory and reduce effective batch size. We recommend token bucketing — group similar-length requests.
[00:02:18] Ravi: we mostly have variable length prompts 50-500 tokens. Any suggestions?
[00:02:22] Elena: two options: 1) enforce a soft truncation or cost-based truncation to keep effective length under 256 for batching, or 2) implement client-side routing that tags short vs long and send to different queues — short queue can use aggressive max_num_seqs. We can share example router config.
[00:02:42] Aisha: how does KV cache interact with batching? we rely on prefix caching for chat stalls.
[00:02:48] Jonas: yeah, good question.
[00:02:50] Elena: KV cache is per session key on the GPU. For continuous batching, if many sessions share the same prefix we can reuse KV cache — that drastically reduces compute. But if sessions are all unique, then KV cache hits are low and you rely more on batching. Also note that warm cache plus large batch can exceed GPU memory; we recommend enabling selective eviction for inactive sessions.
[00:03:12] Lucy: what is selective eviction?
[00:03:15] Elena: it's a policy to evict old KV entries when memory pressure crosses threshold — TTL-based or LRU. You can tune eviction_threshold_percent, for example 70% to start evicting.
[00:03:28] Ravi: any numbers? ballpark improvement with cache hits?
[00:03:31] Samir: With good KV cache hit rate (say 60-70%) we've seen token cost drop by 40-60% on chat-heavy workloads and latency per new token can drop 2-3x since attention compute skips a chunk. But those are workload-dependent.
[00:03:45] Tom: ok. Back to scheduler knobs, what's the recommended starting config for our G5-like fleet?
[00:03:52] Elena: Start with batch_timeout=12ms, max_num_seqs=16, max_tokens_per_batch=4096, token_bucket_windows of 64 tokens. These are conservative for mixed short/medium lengths. If you want more throughput you can raise max_num_seqs to 32 and batch_timeout to 20ms.
[00:04:10] Aisha: does batch_timeout add to p95 latency directly?
[00:04:13] Elena: Yes, it's additive for queued requests. But if the batch forms quickly because of high QPS, the effective wait is low. So if you have steady load (1000 rps) raising batch_timeout is fine. For spiky loads, smaller timeouts are safer.
[00:04:27] Ravi: we have spiky incoming traffic. Our SLA needs keep tail latency tight. So maybe we need hybrid routing.
[00:04:33] Samir: Exactly — hybrid routing: a fast-path with max_num_seqs=8 and lower timeout for latency-sensitive requests; a bulk-path with higher packing for cost efficiency. We'll share the example two-queue config.
[00:04:46] Lucy: about token limits — if we cap to 256 we lose context. Chat continuity is important. any compromise?
[00:04:53] Elena: you can keep a short active context window for online responses and offload long history to a cheap store; during generation use prefix retrieval that's summarized. Or selectively cache only last N tokens in KV and store the rest in external vector DB. That keeps KV small and batchable.
[00:05:12] Ravi: interesting. On quantization: we want to run int8 for cost but worry about quality regression. Thoughts?
[00:05:18] Elena: int8 can give 1.5-2.5x throughput and memory reductions but expect some quality drift especially on instruction-following or long-range dependencies. We recommend running a small eval set — Redwood has a quant_eval kit; we'll share results for target models. fp16/amp gives less throughput uplift but is safer.
[00:05:36] Jonas: any impact on KV accuracy?
[00:05:38] Elena: quantization typically impacts weights not KV retrieval per se, but end-to-end quality changes can affect next-token probabilities. Also mixed-precision kernels may change latency deterministically.
[00:05:49] Tom: what about batching and quantization compatibility?
[00:05:51] Elena: they're compatible; kernel selection prefers int8-optimized fused attention when quantized models are available. But some int8 kernels are slower at tiny batch sizes; so you want sufficient batch volume.
[00:06:05] Aisha: VPC/on-prem specifics: our security team wants to ensure private deployment performance parity with hosted. Any caveats?
[00:06:12] Samir: network egress and storage latency are the big ones. On-prem GPUs often have NVMe or local filesystem latency differences vs cloud. We recommend colocating model weights on local NVMe and ensuring PCIe lanes and torch/cuda drivers match Redwood recommended versions. Also make sure KMS/HSM latency is low if you use envelope encryption during inference.
[00:06:33] Lucy: is there extra tuning for on-prem?
[00:06:35] Elena: yes — disable any remote checkpointing during steady-state inference, pin CPU affinities for scheduler threads, and increase prefetch to hide I/O. We'll provide an on-prem tuning checklist.
[00:06:47] Ravi: can we run a PoC on our on-prem lab?
[00:06:50] Samir: Absolutely. We can either do a remote-managed PoC (Redwood control plane + customer infra) or deliver a Private package. For initial throughput tuning we recommend running native Redwood runtime on your lab with profiling enabled so we can iterate quickly.
[00:07:03] Tom: profiling — what metrics should we gather?
[00:07:06] Elena: tokens/sec, percentiles (50/90/95/99), batch size distribution, KV cache hit rate, GPU occupancy, memory headroom, kernel times (attention, FFN), and scheduler queue times. We have a perf collector agent that exports these as CSV/Prom metrics.
[00:07:21] Ravi: ok, sounds good. any gotchas when measuring?
[00:07:24] Samir: warmup matters — ignore first N minutes of runs. Also measure under realistic request patterns; synthetic uniform requests overestimate batching benefits.
[00:07:36] Lucy: our security team asked about audit logs and RBAC during PoC.
[00:07:39] Samir: Redwood Private includes audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC and KMS integration. We'll share the checklist link in the notes.
[00:07:49] Aisha: about scheduler: you mentioned max_tokens_per_batch — what happens when a single request is very long?
[00:07:55] Elena: If a single request exceeds max_tokens_per_batch it will get its own batch and may block others; we can split long requests into micro-batches or use streaming generation so tokens are emitted early. There's also a hard limit to prevent OOM.
[00:08:08] Ravi: we use streaming extensively. how does streaming interact with batching?
[00:08:12] Elena: streaming can reduce perceived latency by sending early tokens; but for large-batch optimizations you may lose some batching if you stream token-by-token. We support chunked streaming — form a batch for first N tokens and then stream subsequent tokens while maintaining backend efficiency. It is a trade-off.
[00:08:30] Samir: quick interjection: here are the example knobs we'll share — batch_timeout_ms, max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, token_bucket_window, eviction_threshold_percent, prefetch_workers, batch_priority_policy.
[00:08:45] Tom: what's batch_priority_policy?
[00:08:47] Elena: policy to prioritize latency-sensitive queues over bulk ones, can be strict or weighted. Weighted gives some throughput to bulk even when latency queue is present.
[00:08:58] Ravi: do you support on-the-fly config changes? like bump max_num_seqs without restart?
[00:09:02] Elena: yes within reason. Many knobs can be hot-reloaded; others like kernel selection may require a rolling restart to swap binary kernels. We'll mark which ones are hot and which require restart in the config doc.
[00:09:16] Aisha: what about GPU fragmentation with variable model sizes? we run a couple different model families.
[00:09:21] Samir: affinity and worker pools help — pin models to pools sized to their memory footprint. Use model variants (quantized smaller variants) for less-demanding routes. Smart routing can fall back to cheaper variants when capacity tightens.
[00:09:34] Lucy: any examples of throughput gains with multi-model fleets?
[00:09:37] Elena: yes, in a mixed fleet we saw 30-50% better overall token throughput by packing small models together and using quantized variants for less critical routes.
[00:09:46] Ravi: okay, let's talk concrete benchmark plan.
[00:09:48] Samir: we'll share the benchmark sheet. Proposed: baseline run with your current config, then runs with: (A) max_num_seqs=16 batch_timeout=12ms; (B) max_num_seqs=32 batch_timeout=20ms; (C) two-queue hybrid; (D) quantized int8 variant. For each run collect p50/p95/p99 tokens/sec, batch distribution, KV hit rate.
[00:10:12] Tom: timeline?
[00:10:13] Samir: if you can run initial baselines this week, we can iterate and follow up in 2 weeks. We'll prepare the config snippets and RFIs by EOD.
[00:10:22] Ravi: yes we can start.
[00:10:24] Elena: small note: when you try int8, run qualitative evals alongside perf to detect hallucination or instruction-following regressions.
[00:10:33] Ravi: understood.
[00:10:35] Lucy: slightly off-topic: licensing for private deploy — any constraints on kernel mods?
[00:10:40] Samir: Private includes source-level integration for runtime but kernel changes may be gated. We'll surface the agreements in the contract stage.
[00:10:48] Aisha: ok.
[00:10:50] Samir: quick recap of action items and next steps: 1) Redwood share scheduler knob examples + benchmark sheet (Samir) 2) Customer run baseline & variants and upload results (Ravi) 3) Redwood share quant_eval kit and on-prem checklist (Elena) 4) follow-up PoC check in 2 weeks. Anything to add?
[00:11:19] Ravi: no, that's comprehensive.
[00:11:21] Tom: thanks everyone.
[00:11:22] Samir: thanks all. We'll email notes and links.
[00:11:26] [end of recording]
